Annual Meetings

Afternoon Session - 2015 Meeting

Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger explain why they don't think American corporations are taxed too much and discuss the possibility of activists trying to seize control of Berkshire when Buffett is no longer running the company. They also dismiss the argument that a college education boosts lifetime earnings, and Buffett is asked what he would do if he had to give up either his private jet or using the internet.

Sat, May 2 2015 • 1:00 PM EDT
Key Chapters —
  1. 7. No "tears" for corporations on taxes
  2. 12. Reinsurance business getting worse due to "facades"
  3. 16. Why I'm giving away most of my wealth
  4. 21. Munger: GEICO synergies are "dumb idea"
  5. 23. Could activists take control after Buffett?
  6. 28. Buffett values internet more than private jet
  7. 30. "Ridiculous argument" that college boosts lifetime earnings
  8. 33. How Buffett found his first investors
  9. 34. Munger: rationality is a moral virtue
  10. 36. Buffett on fun and "the game"
  11. 37. Dow Jones's big missed opportunity

2. Businesses that do best in high inflation

BECKY QUICK: OK. This is a question â oops, that's not the question. Hold on.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Here it is. This is a question from John Wells, right here in Omaha, and he says, "You've described inflation as a gigantic corporate tapeworm. Which of Berkshire's businesses are best suited to thrive during a period of high inflation and why? Which will suffer the most and why?"

Sync Video to Paragraph

WARREN BUFFETT: Yeah. Well, the best businesses during inflation are usually the best â they're the businesses that you buy once and then you don't have to keep making capital investments subsequently.

Sync Video to Paragraph

So you get â you do not face the problem of continuous reinvestment involving greater and greater dollars because of inflation.

Sync Video to Paragraph

That's one reason real estate, in general, is good during inflation. If you built your own house 55 years ago like Charlie did, or bought one 55 years ago like I did, it's a one-time outlay, whereas if you're â and you get the â you get an inflationary expansion in replacement capital without having to replace yourself.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And if you've got something that's useful to someone else, it tends to be priced in terms of replacement value over time, so you really get the inflationary kick.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Now, if you're in a business such as the utility business or the railroad business, it just keeps eating up more and more money, and your depreciation charges are inadequate and you're kidding yourself as to your real economic profits.

Sync Video to Paragraph

So, any business with heavy capital investment tends to be a poor business to be in in inflation and often it's a poor business to be in generally.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And the business where you buy something once â a brand is a wonderful thing to own during inflation.

Sync Video to Paragraph

You know, See's Candy built their brand many years ago. Now, we've had to nourish it as we've gone along, but the value of that brand increases during inflation, just as the value of, really, any strongly branded goods.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Gillette bought the entire radio rights to the World Series in 1939. And as I remember, it cost them $100,000, and for that they got to broadcast the Yankees, I think, versus the Reds in 1939.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And think of the number of impressions they made on minds in 1939 dollars for $100,000, and they were getting in the minds of young guys like myself. I was eight or nine. And millions of people â and they did it in those dollars then.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And, of course, if you were going to go out and try out and do â have similar impressions on millions of minds now, it'd cost a fortune. And part of that is due to inflation. Part of it's due to other things.

Sync Video to Paragraph

But it was a great investment, which could be made in 1939 dollars that paid off, in terms of selling razors and blades in 1960 and 1970 and 1980 dollars.

Sync Video to Paragraph

So that's the kind of business you want to own.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Charlie?

Sync Video to Paragraph

CHARLIE MUNGER: Well, yeah, but if the inflation ever goes completely out of control, you have no idea how it's going to end up.

Sync Video to Paragraph

If it weren't for the Weimar inflation, we might never have had Adolf Hitler. It was the twosome of the great German inflation followed by the Great Depression that brought us Hitler. And think of the price that the world paid for that one.

Sync Video to Paragraph

We don't want inflation because it's good for See's Candy. (Laughter)

Sync Video to Paragraph

WARREN BUFFETT: I didn't quite realize I was â

Sync Video to Paragraph

CHARLIE MUNGER: No, I wasn't criticizing you.

Sync Video to Paragraph

WARREN BUFFETT: What's good for See's Candy is good for the United States. (Laughter)

5. Climate change risk for insurance subsidiaries

WARREN BUFFETT: Andrew?

Sync Video to Paragraph

ANDREW ROSS SORKIN: Warren, you have said that global warming has not increased Berkshire's payouts for weather-related events. Yet, other insurers, including Travelers, have cited climate change as a risk factor that they use.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Are Berkshire's models different and, if so, how?

Sync Video to Paragraph

WARREN BUFFETT: Yeah. No. I've seen the â of course, the SEC requires you put in all these risk factors, and the lawyers will tell you to put in, you know, everything possibly you can think of, you know, that you'll develop Alzheimer's or whatever it may be.

Sync Video to Paragraph

They just want you to have a laundry list so that it's all been covered in case of later litigation or something of the sort.

Sync Video to Paragraph

So people do put in weather risk, and maybe they put it in because they've got some model that shows it. But, you know, we price our business â basically, we price it every year.

Sync Video to Paragraph

It's not like a life insurance company. A life insurance company you make a contract that â so much a thousand. And if you buy whole life insurance, you've set a price for â if you're 20, you may have set a price for 60 or 70 years in the future. But that is not the property casualty insurance business, which we're in.

Sync Video to Paragraph

We set it one year at a time. And I see nothing that tells me that on a yearly basis that global warming is something that should cause me to change my prices a lot, or even a small amount.

Sync Video to Paragraph

That doesn't mean that it isn't a threat to humanity or â you know, and terribly important. It just means that if I'm going to sell a one-year insurance policy, and I'm going to sell it on a $1 billion plant, I may care enormously about the fire protection, and other various other kinds of protection, within that plant.

Sync Video to Paragraph

I may care about what's going on adjacent to that plant, and all kinds of things, but I am not thinking about global warming. It does not change the situation, in a material way, in any one-year period of time, in my judgment.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And, you know, it â if I was writing a 50-year wind storm policy in Florida, I would think very hard about what global warming might do in that case to the incidence and the intensity of potential hurricanes.

Sync Video to Paragraph

But I do not think it has any material effect on the likelihood of â or the intensity â of a hurricane in Florida or Louisiana or Texas or â next year.

Sync Video to Paragraph

So, it is not a â it's not something I would put in the 10-K as a threat.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Charlie?

Sync Video to Paragraph

CHARLIE MUNGER: I don't think it's totally clear what the effects of global warming will be on extremes of weather. I think there's a lot of guesswork in that field, and a lot of people like howling about calamities that are by no means sure.
